No. 26-426


In the Supreme Court of the United States
_______________
U.S. DEPARTMENT OF HOMELAND SECURITY, ET AL.,
Petitioners,
v.
D.V.D., ET AL.,
Respondents.
_______________
ON WRIT OF CERTIORARI TO THE UNITED STATES
COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE FIRST CIRCUIT
_________________________________
BRIEF OF IOWA AND 20 OTHER STATES
AS AMICI CURIAE SUPPORTING
PETITIONERS
______________________________________________
BRENNA BIRD
  Attorney General of Iowa
ERIC WESSAN
  Solicitor General
  Counsel of Record
1305 E Walnut Street
Des Moines, IA 50319
(515) 823- 9117
eric.wessan@ag.iowa.gov
Counsel for Amici Curiae
(additional counsel listed in addendum)

i

QUESTIONS PRESENTED
The Court directed the parties to brief and argue
the following questions, among others. This brief
addresses the first three.
1. Whether the district court had jurisdiction over
Respondents’ claims.
2. Whether the district court had authority to
enter classwide declaratory relief and APA
vacatur under 8 U.S.C. § 1252(f)(1).
3. Whether the Government’s Guidance on third -
country removals is unlawful under 8 U.S.C.
§ 1231(b), the Due Process Clause, or
FARRA/CAT and its implementing regulations.

ii

INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE
Amici are the States of Iowa, and 20 Additional
States. When the federal government cannot remove
an alien who has been ordered removed, that alien
does not disappear. He lives in one of the States. And
when the alien is a convicted murderer, rapist, or child
abuser whose home country refuses to take him back,
the people who live with the consequences are the
States’ citizens and the State and local officers sworn
to protect them. “The pervasiveness of federal
regulation does not diminish the importance of
immigration policy to the States.” Arizona v. United
States, 567 U.S. 387, 397 (2012).
That importance is at its peak here. Once an
alien’s removal period lapses and removal is not
reasonably foreseeable, the Executive generally must
release him. Zadvydas v. Davis, 533 U.S. 678, 699–701
(2001); Clark v. Martinez, 543 U.S. 371, 378–79 (2005).
Recalcitrant home countries thus  may hold a key to
American jail cells. Third-country removal is how the
Executive takes that key back. Congress authorized
removal to any country “whose government will accept
the alien” when the countries closer to the alien will
not. 8 U.S.C. § 1231(b)(1)(C)(iv), (b)(2)(E)(vii). Without
that option, an alien whose country rejects the return
of a hardened terrorist, rapist, or murderer, the State
Department simply waits out the clock.
The States know what happens next. Take Jean
Jacques. After serving a prison sentence for attempted
murder, he was ordered removed to Haiti. Haiti
rejected three separate requests for travel documents,
and ICE released him. Office of Inspector General,
U.S. Dep’t of Homeland Sec., Investigation into the
Release of Jean Jacques (June 16, 2016),

2

https://perma.cc/6MXW-UR9Q. Months later, Jacques
stabbed 25-year-old Casey Chadwick to death in her
Norwich, Connecticut apartment. Id. ; Feds to
Investigate Why Murder Suspect Wasnt Deported ,
NBC Connecticut  (Jan. 21, 2016) ,
https://bit.ly/4s7k3hK.
Tragically, Jacques is not an outlier on the
federal docket. As of July 2024, ICE reported 662,566
noncitizens with criminal histories on its national
docket, and 13,099 aliens convicted of homicide on its
non-detained docket alone. Letter from Patrick J.
Lechleitner, Deputy Dir., ICE, to Rep. Tony Gonzales
(Sept. 25, 2024), https://perma.cc/2TJX-ZA2T.
The record here tells the same story in
miniature. DHS has used the challenged Guidance to
carry out thousands of third- country removals,
including 103 removals of aliens whose home
countries refused repatriation or who posed public -
safety concerns, 23 of them murderers. Pet.App. 95a–
96a ¶¶ 11– 13. Another 1,432 convicted criminals
await third-country removal, including 139 detained
aliens convicted of offenses like murder, rape, and
child sexual abuse. Pet.App. 94a, 98a ¶¶ 9, 15. Within
days of the First Ci rcuit’s midnight order dissolving
its stay, DHS canceled a flight carrying 70 criminal
aliens to three countries and pulled nearly 150 more
from flights to at least four others. Appl. 2, 40. Every
one of those aliens who cannot be removed may end up
released in a State.
The States also have a structural stake. Many
state and local agencies now partner with ICE to
identify and transfer removable criminal aliens;
Iowa’s Department of Public Safety, for one, signed a
287(g) task -force agreement in March 2025. See

3

Stephen Gruber -Miller, Iowa DPS Signs Agreement
with ICE Creating Immigration Task Force. What It
Will Do: , Des Moines Reg. (Apr. 17, 2025),
https://perma.cc/3CPM-M4D4. Those partnerships
assume that a transfer to federal custody ends in
removal.
And the States depend on Congress’s
jurisdictional lines being enforced as written.
Congress channeled challenges to executing  removal
orders into a single petition for review and forbade
district courts from restraining the removal provisions
on a classwide basis. 8 U.S.C. § § 1252(a)(5), (b)(9),
(f)(1), (g). When courts treat those jurisdictional lines
as suggestions, the national immigration system
bends to the views of a single district judge, and the
States absorb the result.
The Court should reverse.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
For more than a quarter century, the rules for
third-country removal were settled. An alien ordered
removed could be sent to any country willing to take
him when the countries closer to him would not.
8 U.S.C. § 1231(b)(1)(C)(iv), (b)(2)(E)(vii). He could not
be sent to a country where his life or freedom would be
threatened on a protected ground, or where he had an
individualized likelihood of being  tortured. Id.
§ 1231(b)(3)(A); 8 C.F.R. § 208.16(c), 208.17 . And
where the Secretary of State obtained diplomatic
assurances from a receiving country that the Attorney
General found sufficient, the alien’s torture claim was
“not considered further” by anyone. 8 C.F.R.
§ 208.18(c)(3).

4

Congress paired those substantive rules with
an equally deliberate scheme of review: fear -based
objections and challenges to the execution of removal
orders go to a court of appeals on a petition for review,
and no lower court may restrain the removal
provisions on a classwide basis. 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(4),
(a)(5), (b)(9), (f)(1), (g).
The district court discarded both halves of that
design. It entertained a class action that Congress
prohibited, entered classwide declarations and a
universal vacatur that do exactly what Congress
forbade a classwide injunction to do, and read into a
statute that disclaims any “procedural right” a
procedural right that the court then promised to
enforce. 8 U.S.C. § 1231(h). The First Circuit largely
affirmed. The judgment should be reversed for three
independent reasons.
I. The district court lacked jurisdiction. Section
1252(g) strips every court of jurisdiction over “any
cause or claim” arising from “the decision or action” to
“execute removal orders.” Every class member, by
definition, is someone DHS “has deported or will
deport” to a third country, and every claim attacks the
steps DHS takes to do so. The First Circuit escaped
that text by limiting Section 1252(g) to “discretionary”
actions. But the word appears nowhere in the statute,
and the gloss makes jurisdiction turn on the merits.
Sections 1252(a)(4), (a)(5), and (b)(9), and the Foreign
Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act of 1998
(“FARRA”) § 2242(d), independently route these
Convention Against Torture (“ CAT”)-based and
country-of-removal objections to a petition for review.
II. Section 1252(f)(1) barred the classwide
relief. No lower court may “enjoin or restrain” the

5

operation of Section 1231 on a classwide basis, and
“restrain” means to “check, hold back, or prevent.”
Garland v. Aleman Gonzalez, 596 U.S. 543, 549 (2022)
(quotation omitted) . Declarations that every class
member holds an enforceable right to the court’s
preferred procedures, issued with the promise of
follow-on injunctions and enforced the moment the
stay lifted, restrain. A vacatur entered to install those
procedures does to o. A court cannot do in two steps
what Congress forbade it to do in one.
III. The Guidance is lawful. Section 1231(b)(3)
sets a substantive limit on where DHS may send an
alien; it prescribes no procedure, and Section 1231(h)
forbids construing Section 1231 to create one. FARRA
is no different, and the First Circuit’s contrary reading
inverted ordinary interpretation by asking whether
anything precluded the procedures it wanted. The Due
Process Clause adds nothing. The Executive’s
judgment that a foreign sovereign’s assurances are
credible is conclusive, Munaf v. Geren , 553 U.S. 674,
702–703 (2008), and notice, an opportunity to claim
fear, and prompt screening are ample process for
aliens who already had full removal proceedings.
The Court should reverse the judgment of the
court of appeals.

6


ARGUMENT
I. THE DISTRICT COURT LACKED
JURISDICTION BECAUSE CONGRESS
CHANNELED EVERY CLAIM ABOUT
EXECUTING A REMOVAL ORDER AWAY FROM
THE DISTRICT COURTS.
In 1996, Congress replaced a judicial -review
regime that had invited piecemeal litigation over
every stage of deportation with one that sends
removal-related claims down a single path. Reno v.
American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Comm., 525 U.S.
471, 475–476, 486–487 (1999) (“AADC”).
Two features of that design decide this case.
Section 1252(g) withdraws jurisdiction over claims
arising from three specified actions, including the
execution of removal orders. And Sections 1252(a)(4),
(a)(5), and (b)(9), backed by FARRA § 2242(d), channel
what remains, including every CAT claim and every
question of law or fact arising from an action to remove
an alien, into a petition for review. Respondents’ suit
runs headlong into both.
A. Section 1252(g) Bars “Any” Claim Arising
From An Action To Execute A Removal
Order, Not Just Claims Attacking
Discretion.
This Court has long issued a call to read
unambiguous text to do what the text says .
“[N]otwithstanding any other provision of law
(statutory or nonstatutory),” “no court shall have
jurisdiction to hear any cause or claim by or on behalf

7

of any alien arising from the decision or action by the
Attorney General to commence proceedings,
adjudicate cases, or execute removal orders against
any alien.” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(g). This Court has read
that law to cover “three discrete actions.” AADC , 525
U.S. at 482. Executing a removal order is one of them.
Respondents’ claims straightforwardly arise
from challenging an executed removal order . The
certified class consists of aliens with final removal
orders “whom DHS has deported or will deport” to a
third country. Pet.App. 106a.
An alien whose removal order DHS is not
executing is excluded from  the class. And the only
aspect Respondents challenge is how DHS goes about
executing those orders: which notice it gives, how long
it waits, and whether it may rely on a receiving
country’s assurances before putting the alien on the
plane. A removal order “does not limit the authority
of” DHS “to remove the alien to any other country as
permitted by” Section 1231(b) when removal to the
designated country fails. 8 C.F.R.  § 1240.12(d).
Choosing that country, and moving the alien there, is
executing the order.
AADC confirms that point. The plaintiffs there
alleged that the government had targeted them for
removal in violation of the First Amendment. 525 U.S.
at 473– 474. That is a claim that the Executive
exceeded a legal limit on its authority. The Court still
held that it fell “squarely within § 1252(g).” Id. at 487.
If an alleged constitutional violation in commencing
proceedings is a claim “arising from” the
commencement of proceedings, an alleged procedural
violation in executing a removal order is a claim

8

“arising from” its execution. After all, the Constitution
reigns supreme.
The First Circuit avoided that conclusion by
holding that Section 1252(g) reaches only
“discretionary” decisions, and that the Executive has
no discretion to violate the law. Pet. App. 119a, 122a.
That limitation fails for three reasons.
First, it is not in the statute. Section 1252(g)
covers “any cause or claim” arising from “the decision
or action” to execute removal orders. Congress knows
how to confine review bars to discretion when it wants
to. See 8 U.S.C. § 1226(e) (“ The Attorney General’s
discretionary judgment regarding the application of
this section shall not be subject to review”); 8 U.S.C.
§ 1252(a)(2)(B) (barring review of certain “[d]enials of
discretionary relief”). It did not do so here. The courts
of appeals that have looked at the text have said so.
See E.F.L. v. Prim, 986 F.3d 959, 965 (7th Cir. 2021);
Rauda v. Jennings , 55 F.4th 773, 777– 778 (9th Cir.
2022).
Second, the gloss makes jurisdiction depend on
the merits. Under the First Circuit’s rule, a court may
hear the claim only if the Executive acted unlawfully,
and it can know whether the Executive acted
unlawfully only by hearing the claim. This Court has
rejected that circularity in this very statutory scheme.
Aleman Gonzalez, 596 U.S. at 554.
Third, the gloss swallows the rule. Nearly every
claim against the execution of a removal order can be
pleaded as a claim that the Executive breached some
statutory, regulatory, or constitutional duty.
Respondents did exactly that. If pleading illegality
unlocks the courthouse, Section 1252(g)  protects

9

nothing but the lawful exercise of discretion, which no
one would challenge anyway. Congress does not enact
jurisdictional bars that bar only suits plaintiffs would
lose.
The First Circuit’s two other moves fare no
better. It reasoned that Respondents challenge a
decision not to execute the country -designation
portion of their orders. Pet. App. 116a, 118a. But
removal to a third country under 8 C.F.R. § 1240.12(d)
is an execution of the order, and a claim that DHS is
executing an order the wrong way still “aris[es] from”
the decision to execute it.
Nor can invoking  Department of Homeland
Security v. Regents of the University of California, 591
U.S. 1, 19 (2020) , save the First Circuit’s analysis .
Pet.App. 119a. Regents involved the rescission of a
deferred-action program that conferred work
authorization and other benefits, a programmatic
choice the Court found was not a decision to
commence, adjudicate, or execute anything. 591 U.S.
at 19. The challenged Guidance here governs nothing
but the execution of final removal orders.
B. Sections 1252(a)(4), (a)(5), And (b)(9) And
FARRA Channel Fear-Based Objections
To A Country Of Removal Into A Petition
For Review.
Even if Section 1252(g) left any room,  and it
does not,  the INA’s channeling provisions fill it.
“Judicial review of all questions of law and fact,
including interpretation and application of
constitutional and statutory provisions, arising from
any action taken or proceeding brought to remove an
alien from th e United States” is available “only in

10

judicial review of a final order under this section.”
8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(9).
A petition for review is “the sole and exclusive
means for judicial review of any cause or claim under”
CAT. Id. § 1252(a)(4). And FARRA explains  that
nothing in it confers jurisdiction “to consider or review
claims raised under the Convention .  . . or any other
determination made with respect to the application of
the policy,” “except as part of the review of a final
order of removal.” FARRA § 2242(d), 112 Stat. 2681-
822; see 8 C.F.R. 208.18(e)(1).
Respondents’ suit is built on CAT and on
objections to the country of removal. Its premise is
that class members have a right to raise torture and
persecution claims against a newly designated
country before removal. That is a “cause or claim
under” CAT, a nd a question of law “arising from” an
“action taken .  . . to remove an alien.” The district
court itself once described the relief Respondents
sought as “based on” FARRA. D.V.D. v. U.S. Dept. of
Homeland Sec. , 778 F. Supp. 3d 355, 379 (D. Mass.
2025).
Nor is the channeled path  to a petition for
review illusory. Under the Guidance, an alien who
expresses fear and satisfies the screening standard is
referred to the immigration court, through reopening
where necessary. Pet. App. 85a, 87a. That route ends
in an administrative decision reviewable on a petition
for review, which is exactly where Congress wanted
these claims heard. See Nasrallah v. Barr, 590 U.S.
573, 582– 585 (2020). DHS has long agreed to join
motions to reopen in appropriate third -country cases.
70 Fed. Reg. 661, 671 (Jan.  5, 2005). Government
counsel described that very route to the First Circuit.

11

Pet.App. 30a n.49. A procedural objection to how the
screening was conducted can travel up with the
merits.
The First Circuit held that Section 1252(a)(4)
reaches only claims for which CAT itself supplies the
cause of action. Pet.App. 124a–126a; see Pet.App. 31a–
32a. But CAT is not self -executing and creates no
cause of action at all. On the First Circuit’s reading,
Section 1252(a)(4) applies to nothing. The court’s
rejoinder, that the law still bars CAT claims in habeas,
Pet.App. 124a, ignores that Section 1252(a)(4)
displaces “any other provision of law (statutory or
nonstatutory), including section 2241 . . . or any other
habeas corpus provision.” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(4)
(emphasis added). “Including” marks habeas as one
example, not the whole set. Scalia & Garner, Reading
Law 132 (2012). And the APA is just as much an “other
provision of law.”
The First Circuit likewise read Sections
1252(a)(5) and (b)(9) out of the case because
Respondents do not seek “review of an order of
removal, the decision to seek removal, or the process
by which removability is determined.” Pet. App. 129a.
That language comes from the Jennings  plurality’s
description of claims, like challenges to prolonged
detention, that are only tangentially related to
removal. Jennings v. Rodriguez , 583 U.S. 281, 293–
294 (2018) (plurality opinion).
But Respondents’ claims here go to the core of
removal itself: where, when, and how the alien is sent
abroad. Questions about the country of removal have
been part of removal proceedings for decades. See 8
C.F.R. § 1240.10(f), 1240.12(d).

12

C. The First Circuit’s Narrowing
Constructions Would Gut A Channeling
Scheme The States Depend On.
The stakes reach well beyond this case.
Congress enacted Section 1252 to end the
“deconstruction, fragmentation, and hence
prolongation of removal proceedings.” AADC, 525 U.S.
at 487. The First Circuit’s approach unfortunately
reimposes all three issues.
Under it, any class of aliens may file an APA
suit in a district court of its choosing, plead that the
Executive has violated a procedural duty in executing
removal orders, and obtain nationwide relief
governing how removals proceed. Today the subject is
third-country removal. Tomorrow it will be the timing
of removal flights, the form of travel documents, or the
content of a notice of removal. Every step in executing
a removal order could be relitigated in a district court
before it happens.
The States are directly hit by  that
fragmentation. Each new round of collateral litigation
delays removals, and each delay pushes more criminal
aliens past the point where  this Court has said
detention must end. Zadvydas, 533 U.S. at 701.
Congress already decided where these claims belong.
This Court should hold that the district court had no
jurisdiction to hear them.
II. SECTION 1252(F)(1) BARS CLASSWIDE
ORDERS THAT “RESTRAIN” THIRD-COUNTRY
REMOVALS, WHATEVER THE LABEL.
Clever labeling cannot evade Congress’s metes
of jurisdiction. “Regardless of the nature of the action

13

or claim or of the identity of the party or parties
bringing the action,” no court other than this one
“shall have jurisdiction or authority to enjoin or
restrain the operation of” the INA’s removal
provisions, “other than with respect to the application
of such provisions to an individual alien.” 8 U.S.C.
§ 1252(f)(1).
Section 1231(b), which authorizes third-country
removal, is among the covered sections . Aleman
Gonzalez, 596 U.S. at 550– 551. The statute thus
“generally prohibits lower courts from entering
injunctions that order federal officials to take or to
refrain from taking actions to enforce, implement, or
otherwise carry out the specified statutory
provisions.” Id. at 550. And it does so even when the
plaintiffs say the officials are violating the statute or
the Constitution. Id. at 552–554.
The district court here did not enter an
injunction despite clearly intending to stop these
third-country removals . And that had a purpose .
Having been stayed twice by this Court, it
acknowledged that it “could be missing something,”
and so swapped its injunction for a set of classwide
declarations and a universal vacatur, pointing to the
“different relief.” Pet. App. 78a. This Court has not
countenanced such clever attempts to repeatedly
evade its emergency docket decisions . See Nat’l
Republican Cong. Comm. v. Brown , No. 26A274, 610
U.S. ___, 2026 WL 2618462 (Sept. 4, 2026).

14

A. “Restrain” Reaches Coercive
Declarations That Dictate How Officers
Must Execute Removal Orders.
Section 1252(f)(1) uses two verbs. “Enjoin”
covers injunctions. “Restrain” is broader: it reaches
orders that “check, hold back, or prevent” the covered
provisions’ operation. Aleman Gonzalez , 596 U.S. at
549 (quotation marks omitted). Any classwide order
that does that “restrain[s]” covered removals  falls
within the bar, however it is styled.
The declarations here do that work. They
declare that every class member has “the right to
meaningful notice before removal to any third
country” and “the right to a meaningful opportunity to
raise a country -specific claim against removal before
removal to any third country.” Pet. App. 81a. Those
declarations speak to DHS, announcing what it must
do before it may carry out Section 1231(b). And they
leave the content of “meaningful” to the same court
that, at the preliminary -injunction stage, created its
own judicial impositions under  the same word to
require at least ten days to raise a fear claim, 72 hours’
notice of each interview, and fifteen days to seek
reopening. DVD v. DHS , 2025 WL 1453640, at *1
(D. Mass. May 21, 2025) ; D.V.D. v. U.S. Dept. of
Homeland Sec., 2025 WL 1453604 at *1 (D. Mass. May
5, 2025); 778 F. Supp. 3d at 393.
The declarations come with teeth. A declaratory
judgment is the foundation for “[f]urther necessary or
proper relief,” including an injunction, against any
adverse party whose rights it declares. 28 U.S.C.
§ 2202. So every class member holds a ready -made
basis for an individual injunction the moment DHS
follows its own Guidance instead of the court’s. See

15

Alli v. Decker, 650 F.3d 1007, 1020 n.2 (3d Cir. 2011)
(Fuentes, J., dissenting in part). Just because the
classwide restraint takes two steps rather than one
does not render it any less of a “restrain[t].”
No one in this case has treated the declarations
as advisory. Respondents filed an “emergency” motion
at 8:20 p.m. asking the First Circuit to dissolve its
stay, and the court granted it at 11:36 p.m. without
waiting for the government. Pet. App. 154a.
Respondents then told this Court that the government
must comply immediately. Stay Opp. 2, 9, 34. And
DHS did comply: it canceled a flight carrying 70
criminal aliens to three countries and pulled nearly
150 more from scheduled removals. Appl. 2, 40. Relief
that grounds removal flights within hours “check[s],
hold[s] back, [and] prevent[s]” the operation of Section
1231(b).
This Court has long refused to let a declaratory
label defeat a limit on injunctions. The Tax Injunction
Act forbids district courts to “enjoin, suspend or
restrain” state tax collection, and the Court held that
it bars declaratory judgments, which “may in  every
practical sense operate to suspend collection of the
state taxes until the litigation is ended.” California v.
Grace Brethren Church , 457 U.S. 393, 408 (1982)
(quotation omitted). Where an injunction against state
proceedings would be barred, “declaratory relief
should ordinarily be denied as well.” Samuels v.
Mackell, 401 U.S. 66, 72–73 (1971). And an order with
the “practical effect” of an injunction is treated as one.
Abbott v. Perez , 585 U.S. 579, 594 (2018). The same
verb (“restrain”) and the same substance -over-form
logic govern here.

16

The First Circuit dismissed Grace Brethren as a
federalism case. Pet.App. 149a. But whether a
declaration operates like an injunction does not
depend on whether the restrained sovereign is a State
or the United States. If anything, Section 1252(f)(1)
speaks more emphatically than the Tax Injunction
Act: it applies “[r]egardless of the nature of the action
or claim.”
That reading forbids what Congress forbade:
classwide orders that, in substance, dictate how the
Executive must carry out the covered law.
B. A Classwide Vacatur Entered To Install
The Court’s Procedures Restrains Just
The Same.
The Court need not decide whether Section
1252(f)(1) reaches every vacatur of every agency action
touching the covered provisions, a question it has
twice reserved. Biden v. Texas, 597 U.S. 785, 801 n.4
(2022); Aleman Gonzalez , 596 U.S. at 551 n.2. The
vacatur here is a narrow case. It was entered on behalf
of a certified class of aliens, alongside declarations
prescribing the procedures DHS must use instead, to
accomplish what the stayed injunction had
accomplished. Pet.App. 78a–81a.
The vacated documents confer no authority.
They tell officers how to exercise authority Congress
already gave them. Vacating them leaves officers with
the statute, the regulations, and a judgment declaring
what the court believes the statute requires.
The First Circuit called vacatur “less drastic”
because it “neither compels nor restrains further
agency decision-making.” Pet.App. 151a. That may be
true sometimes. But it is not true of a vacatur whose

17

only function, paired with a declaration of the
replacement procedures, is to stop DHS from
executing removal orders.
C. Respondents’ “Doublet” Theory Reads
“Restrain” Out Of The Statute.
Respondents’ principal answer is that “enjoin or
restrain” is a legal doublet meaning only injunctions
and restraining orders. Stay Opp. 14. The statute’s
neighbors refute that. The very next paragraph
explains that “no court shall enjoin the removal of any
alien” absent a heightened showing, and it uses
“enjoin” alone. 8 U.S.C. § 1252(f)(2).
It is implausible that Congress meant to leave
temporary restraining orders free under paragraph (2)
while barring them under paragraph (1). The better
inference is that “enjoin” already covers injunctive
orders of every duration, and that “restrain” in
paragraph (1) adds something: coercive relief that
does an injunction’s work under another name. See
Aleman Gonzalez, 596 U.S. at 549. Had the doublet
theory been obvious, this Court would not have twice
left the question open.
Respondents also point to Section 1252(e)(1)(A),
which bars “declaratory, injunctive, or other equitable
relief” in a different context. Stay Opp. 13. But that
section is framed by remedy, while Section 1252(f)(1)
is framed by effect: it bars orders that “restrain the
operation of” the statute. Congress listed remedies in
one provision and described a function in the other. A
declaration that does not restrain is not barred. A
declaration that does is.
Nor does that  reading leave aliens without a
remedy. Section 1252(f)(1) preserves relief “with

18

respect to the application of such provisions to an
individual alien,” and it leaves this Court’s authority
intact. The district court should have respected that
choice.
III. THE GUIDANCE IS LAWFUL.
The Guidance tracks the line Congress drew.
DHS may not remove an alien to a country where he
would likely be persecuted on a protected ground or
tortured. So before a third -country removal, DHS
either relies on a receiving country’s assurances that
the St ate Department finds credible, or it gives the
alien written notice, waits at least 24 hours, and
screens any fear he expresses, referring him to the
immigration court if he meets the standard. Pet. App.
84a–87a. None of  the INA, FARRA, nor the
Constitution requires more.
A. Section 1231(b) Sets A Substantive Limit
And Leaves Procedure To The Executive.
Section 1231(b)(3)(A) explains  that the
Attorney General “may not remove an alien to a
country if the Attorney General decides that the
alien’s life or freedom would be threatened in that
country” on a protected ground. That is a limit on
outcomes. It says nothing about notice periods,
interviews, or adjudicators. And where a statute
imposes a substantive obligation without prescribing
procedures, the agency, not a court, decides how to
meet it. Vermont Yankee Nuclear Power Corp.  v.
NRDC, Inc., 435 U.S. 519, 543–544 (1978).
Congress did not leave that  conclusion to
inference. It added: “Nothing in this section shall be
construed to create any substantive or procedural

19

right or benefit that is legally enforceable by any party
against the United States or its agencies or officers or
any other person.” 8 U.S.C. § 1231(h). The courts
construed Section 1231 to create a procedural right,
legally enforceable by a class of aliens against DHS.
But the statute itself precludes that result.
The district court rested on the presumption of
“congressional solicitude for fair procedure, absent
explicit statutory language to the contrary.” Pet. App.
49a (quoting Califano v. Yamasaki, 442 U.S. 682, 693
(1979)). The district court failed to wrestle with
section 1231(h) , though, which is explicit statutory
language to the contrary. The presumption the district
court invoked defeats its own conclusion.
The First Circuit, for its part, candidly read
Section 1231(b) “to mean more than what [it] plainly
say[s].” Pet.App. 137a. Constitutional avoidance lets a
court choose between plausible readings of the text
and confers no “license to graft” new requirements
“onto the text.” Jennings, 583 U.S. at 298. This Court
reversed the Ninth Circuit in Jennings  for reading
bond hearings into detention statutes that contained
none. Id. at 296–306. The First Circuit did the same
as to notice periods and hearings here.
The practical rationale  fueling the decision
before the Court today  fares no better. The First
Circuit reasoned that DHS cannot know whether a
particular alien faces persecution without the alien’s
input. Pet.App. 49a, 137a.
But for an assurance country, the receiving
government has represented that it will not persecute
or torture anyone removed there, and the State
Department has found that representation credible.

20

Pet.App. 84a. A credible assurance that applies to
every removed alien necessarily applies to each one.
For any other country, the Guidance does  seek the
alien’s input: it screens any fear he raises  as to a
country that he may be sent. Pet.App. 85a–87a.
B. FARRA Does Not Silently Import The
Procedures The First Circuit Read Into
Section 1231(b).
FARRA states a policy against returning
anyone to a country where he would likely be tortured
and directs agencies to prescribe implementing
regulations. FARRA § 2242(a)–(b), 112 Stat. 2681-822.
It sets no procedures of its own. And it forecloses
judicial review outside a petition for review. Id.
§ 2242(d).
The agencies wrote those regulations in 1999,
and the regulations settle the question Respondents
raise. When the Secretary of State obtains assurances
that an alien would not be tortured in a country, and
the Attorney General finds them sufficiently relia ble,
“the alien’s claim for protection under the Convention
Against Torture shall not be considered further by an
immigration judge, the Board of Immigration Appeals,
or an asylum officer.” 8 C.F.R. § 208.18(c)(3).
For more than 25 years, then, the CAT
framework has permitted removal on the strength of
diplomatic assurances without any individual
hearing. And the regulations’ judicial-review provision
disclaims creating “a private right of action.” 8 C.F.R.
208.18(e)(2).
The First Circuit nonetheless held that FARRA
requires notice and an opportunity to be heard,
reasoning that “there is no explicit language in the

21

FARRA/CAT or related regulations that precludes”
that reading. Pet. App. 143a. That inverts statutory
interpretation. Courts ask what a statute requires, not
whether it forbids what a court would like to add. The
question is especially apt for the INA, a
“comprehensive and reticulated statute” that should
not “be supplemen ted by extratextual remedies.”
Hughes Aircraft Co.  v. Jacobson , 525 U.S. 432, 447
(1999) (quotation marks omitted).
The court then reasoned that because the same
regulations govern withholding and CAT claims, its
reading of Section 1231(b) must carry over to FARRA.
Pet.App. 144a (citing Clark v. Martinez , 543 U.S. 371
(2005)). That bootstraps one error onto another. It
assumes the Section 1231(b)  holding is right, and it
lets a shared regulation dictate the meaning of a
statute. Cf. Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603
U.S. 369 (2024). If the shared regulations prove
anything, it is that the Executive has long read both
to permit removal on assurances without more
process.
C. The Due Process Clause Requires
Nothing More Than The Guidance
Provides.
1. The Executive’s acceptance of a foreign
sovereign’s assurances is conclusive.
Whether a foreign government will keep its
word is a judgment the Constitution commits to the
political branches. In Munaf v. Geren, this Court held
that federal courts could not block the transfer of two
American citizens to Iraqi custody based on fears of
torture, because the political branches had
determined that the transfer was appropriate. 553
U.S. at 702–703.

22

The Judiciary “is not suited to second- guess
such determinations,” which “would require federal
courts to pass judgment on foreign justice systems and
undermine the Government’s ability to speak with one
voice in this area.” Id.  at 702. If that is true for
citizens, it is true “a fortiori” for aliens with no right
to remain. Kiyemba v. Obama, 561 F.3d 509, 517–518
(D.C. Cir. 2009) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring); see id. at
514 (majority opinion).
Respondents answer that Munaf  involved
individualized assurances. Stay Opp. 30 –31. Nothing
in Munaf turned on that. And whether a sovereign’s
assurance should cover one person or everyone is itself
a diplomatic judgment: it depends on what a foreign
government will agree to, on what terms, and with
what consequences if it breaks its word.
Courts are no better positioned to second-guess
the scope of the Executive’s judgment than its
substance. The district court demanded  to know
“[w]hom do they cover? What do they cover? Why has
the Government deemed them credible?” Pet.App. 3a.
That is a demand to put the State Department’s
diplomacy on trial in a Boston courtroom. The
Secretary of State has explained that third -country
arrangements are “a delicate diplomatic endeavor”
that judicial intervention threatens. Pet.App. 88a–90a
¶¶ 3, 6–8.
Respondents’ objection also mistakes substance
for procedure. Their real complaint is that a
categorical assurance should not suffice to show that
a particular alien is safe. That is a challenge to the
substantive standard, “recast in ‘procedural due
process’ terms.” Reno v. Flores, 507 U.S. 292, 308
(1993). Once the Executive has made the substantive

23

determination, an individual hearing would examine
nothing the standard makes relevant. “Process is not
an end in itself.” Olim v. Wakinekona , 461 U.S. 238,
250 (1983).
2. Notice, a chance to claim fear, and
prompt screening are ample process for
aliens already ordered removed.
For countries without assurances, the Guidance
requires written notice of the country of removal,
explained to the alien; a wait of generally at least 24
hours; and, if the alien expresses fear, a screening by
USCIS, generally within 24 hours, with referral to the
immigration court if he shows that persecution or
torture is more likely than not. Pet.App. 85a–87a.
That extra process comes on top of everything
the class has already received. Every class member
has a final removal order, entered after proceedings in
which he could designate a country, contest
removability, and seek protection. 778 F. Supp. 3d at
378. The only question left is the destination.
In that posture, the Guidance’s process is
constitutionally ample. It mirrors in timing the
expedited-removal screening that this Court upheld
against a due -process challenge. Dept.  of Homeland
Sec. v. Thuraissigiam, 591 U.S. 103, 138– 140 (2020).
And many class members have never been lawfully
admitted. For them, “the decisions of executive or
administrative officers, acting within powers
expressly conferred by Congress, are due process of
law.” Nishimura Ekiu v. United States, 142 U.S. 651,
660 (1892).
The district court distinguished Thuraissigiam
as an admissibility case, Pet. App. 55a –56a, but the

24

alien there also sought additional process for his
withholding and CAT claims, and the Court rejected
his due-process claim in full. 591 U.S. at 118, 138–140.
Respondents lean on A.A.R.P. v. Trump , 605
U.S. 91 (2025) (per curiam). Stay Opp. 27–28, 31. That
case involved detainees facing summary removal
under the Alien Enemies Act who needed enough time
to file habeas petitions contesting whether the Act
applied to them at all. 605 U.S. at 94– 95. The
protection due process affords an alien “may vary
depending upon status and circumstance.” Zadvydas,
533 U.S. at 694.
An alien whose removability was finally
adjudicated years ago, and who now learns only where
he will go, stands in a very different place. The same
is true of Kossov v. INS, 132 F.3d 405 (7th Cir. 1998),
and Andriasian v. INS, 180 F.3d 1033 (9th Cir. 1999),
on which the district court relied. Pet. App. 2a. Those
cases involved aliens who received no meaningful
chance to contest a country first designated at the end
of their hearings. The Guidance gives notice and a
chance to raise fear before removal.
Nor did the government concede otherwise. The
district court quoted government counsel’s statement
in Riley v. Bondi  that the government would give
notice and an opportunity to raise fear before a third -
country removal. Pet. App. 2a. That is what the
Guidance provides for every country that has not
given assurances. The assurance framework, which
the CAT regulations have recognized since 1999, was
not at issue in that exchange.
The district court’s alternative, finally, has no
stopping point. Its final judgment requires a

25

“meaningful” opportunity without saying what that
means. Pet.App. 81a. Its last attempt to say so
produced a 10 -day fear window, a 72- hour interview
notice, and a 15 -day reopening period, about 25 days
of delay for any alien who voices fear, however
frivolous. For an alien whose home country has
refused him, that de lay can unravel a negotiated
removal and run out the clock that Zadvydas starts.
When it does, the alien is released, and a State
inherits him. The Constitution does not require that
result.
CONCLUSION
The Court should reverse the judgment of the
court of appea ls and remand with instructions to
dismiss.
